content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposed a distributed recurrent auto-encoder for image compression that uses a ConvLSTM to learn binary codes that are constructed progressively from residuals of previously encoded information. Experiments show that the proposed model achieved better PSNR than other compression auto-encoders and algorithms. The paper claims distributed representation has advantage for image compression.

The idea in the paper is a good one, except for the part about "distributed". 2 main concerns here:

1. The paper uses the word "distributed" to mean multi-source or clustered data inputs. This is different from what the deep learning community normally means, and the paper has the risk of misleading readers without clarification or using a different terminology. Why not multi-source / multi-modal?

2. By analyzing figure 4 and figure 5 together, it seems that the PSNR results are similar between multi-source / clustered data and normal auto-encoder. The paper mentioned that the multi-source model may have advantage over information corruption and balance between encoder/decoder model sizes, but no experiments are shown to demonstrate that. This rendered the motivation of the whole "distributed" part unclear.

Since the "distributed" seems to occupy a significant portion of the paper, I vote for rejection based on the current manuscript.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
1. We are not working on the "distributed" most widely used in deep learning contexts. Multi-source / multi-modal is perhaps more accurate to describe our work. We had to use 'distributed' mainly because our work is motivated by classical theories in information theory where the DSC is under the "distributed" keyword. We also have detailed discussions about Distributed Source Coding (DSC) in the related work section, thus we believe using "distributed" is still appropriate in this work.

2. We can achieve the theoretical upper bound with normal auto-encoder and all data available (joint distribution known). The application of DSC is where each encoder does not have enough computational power and bandwidth to transmit all the data sources to the server. We can naively train separate auto-encoder for each data source (marginal distribution known). If the data sources are correlated, we cannot achieve the theoretical limit. However, DSC shows that a joint decoder is sufficient. The drawbacks of classical DSC applications is that we cannot design codes for arbitrary correlated data sources. Our work attempts to use deep learning models to train a data-driven DSC. Our results show that data-drive DSC can achieve theoretical limit given arbitrary correlated data sources. Our work also have other advantages like robust distributed encoding where synchronization of data sources is not needed during evaluation. We address low complexity coding issue by showing training half encoders at lower compression qualities. To better address this issue, in the future, we will experiment encoder with less number of parameters.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
The authors propose a method to train image compression models on multiple sources, with a separate encoder on each source, and a shared decoder. The model is based on a recurrent image compression network. The main difference from a standard image compression network is that it has multiple copies of encoders and at training time, it optimizes on all sources jointly. The experiments are conducted on the CIFAR10, MNIST, and Kodak dataset. It shows that the method works slightly worse than jointly training all sources, and clearly outperforms training separate models.

The paper is clearly written and easy to follow. The proposed method is simple. 

My main concerns are regarding the experiment results: 
1. The experiments are conducted on a not very realistic setting of splitting CIFAR10 and MNIST by class labels. First of all these datasets are small, simple, and low-resolution. Second, by splitting by the labels, the sources are still highly correlated as they are collected from the same distribution. Jointly training multiple larger datasets that show more diverse properties would make the results more convincing. 
2. I don't find the motivations of training multiple encoders clear. Given the fact that jointly training on a larger dataset typically gives a better performance, it's still not clear when we would want to train separate encoders. An extended discussion would help.
3. I found the results not very surprising. The observations that a jointly trained model sees more examples, so performs 
better seems expected  (particularly when the dataset is small). 
4. The technical contributions are light-weight. Using multiple copies of parameters for different data distributions is used e.g., in multi-task learning and domain adaptation literatures. 

Overall I think this paper would benefit from improving the experiments and providing better supporting evidence for demonstrating practical value of the system.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
1. Our experiment is designed to show a promising application of Distributed Source Coding (DSC) with Deep Learning models. We train on CIFAR10 dataset and evaluate it on Kodak dataset which is a standard image compression test set. Our model also outperforms Toderic's work. We show the correlation measurement of MNIST dataset in the updated version. Since the split data sources are moderately correlated, it is possible to achieve the theoretical limit where we compress all data with a single encoder. Indeed, we would like to try larger dataset like CIFAR100 and ImageNet, but we find that the correlations of data sources split from CIFAR10 dataset are negligible. Therefore, we choose to use MNIST dataset to show the advantage of DSC.

2. Our work is motivated by the emerging need for less communication and storage complexity in distributed computing. Realistic applications would be similar to those in the context of classical DSC. In particular, each separate encoder may not have the computational power and bandwidth to transmit all the data to the server. A DSC framework is used to design separate encoders for each user and a single decoder for the server. Though it has been theoretically proved that a single decoder is enough to reconstruct separate data sources as if all data are transmitted to the server to design an single source coding scheme, there has not been a practical solution for arbitrary correlated data sources. Although we can always train on a large dataset like ImageNet in advance to design generic codec like JPEG, our experiments on MNIST actually show that training on specific data domain can significantly outperform generic codec.

3. If all the data are available, a single encoder-decoder model indeed performs the best (i.e. theoretical limit). If we have multiple data sources and unlimited amount of data (marginal distribution known), we can achieve the theoretical limit only if they are independent. However, the interesting part shown by DSC is that if they are correlated, we only need a single decoder but possible multiple encoders to achieve the theoretical limit. Meanwhile, although our model is jointly trained, each encoder actually trained separately because the gradient information is only summed over their corresponding batch of data.

4. It is tempting to use different model parameters for different data distributions. Our work shows that a single decoder is sufficient to achieve the same performance as that a single model with all data available. In practice, this is crucial in areas like multi-camera video coding and sensor networks where each encoder has limited computational power and bandwidth. We believe we are the first work that attempts to apply DSC with data-driven models. We do hope to conduct more large-scale experiments in the future.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper presents a method based on Convolutional LSTM that achieves compression of very small resolution images (e.g., 32x32). In this setting it achieves what may be seen as SoTA performance for its class (i.e., recurrent, progressive). The authors also look into applying this method in the setting of distributed source coding.

I think we may want to accept this paper because I have not seen any such work before (though, I have to say I have never encountered distributed source coding problems before; but I have extensively studied neural image approaches).

The paper uses a framework very similar to that of Toderici et al., and it applies the modified architecture to CIFAR and MNIST (the original method was never tested on those datasets by the authors). In this paper that method is outperformed by the proposed architecture, and results are presented in the case in which multiple signals need to be encoded together. Since I am not familiar with the field of DSC, I cannot comment how important this is for that community.

With respect to the evaluation on CIFAR and MNIST, I have soem concerns. In particular, most containers (JPEG, JPEG 2K, BPG) have a considderably sized header. When dealing with such small images, this header may take a significant part of the size of the file. I don't see the authors discussing this, and describing how they adjusted the bitrates for those codecs. Moreover, for datasets like CIFAR, JPEG and BPG are not able to operate properly unless they're set to run in 4:4:4 mode (it's by default using 4:2:0, which puts them at a huge disadvantage). Therefore, I don't know whether I can trust parts of the evaluation, since the authors didn't call out any of these issues.

Moreover, it's not clear what PSNR refers to. I can guess that it may be PSNR in the RGB color space, but this is not called out.

The figures are also poorly labeled. For example, in Figure 4, it's not explicitly said which datasets are used (e.g., I am *guessing* it's CIFAR and MNIST, but it's not clear). The caption for Figure 5 should also be updated, and honestly, I don't think anyone can read the various labels in the charts presented in that figure if printed on a piece of paper, unless they have a looking glass...

I also find it disturbing to be reading an image compression paper with NO COMPRESSED IMAGES SHOWN! I have no idea qualitatively whether this method is any good. In the final version I expect to see images compressed both in the multiple channel setup, and in the single channel setup. I expect to see images compressed with the codecs to be compared against at comparable bitrates, while taking into account to remove the headers and make sure that 4:4:4 mode is enabled, and that a hyperparameter sweep is attempted.

If this paper is to be accepted, the evaluation section needs to be absolutely clear and all points I mentioned need to be addressed.

On the novelty side of things, since it's a tweak on an existing method, I am not very excited, and since I know nothing on DSC, I can't comment on the novelty in that area. I'll defer that judgement to the other reviwers, who hopefully have more insight into this than I do.

Overall, I think it's an interesting twist on an existing type of method, and may be worth publishing ASSUMING that the authors address the problems I mentioned earlier.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
1. Since our main focus is not to build a new generic image codec, we demonstrate our results based on previous deep learning based compression models. To our best knowledge, none of them mentioned overhead of classical codecs. Our results about JPEG and BPG on Kodak dataset are taken from previous work. The main issue we want to address is that a generic codec can be outperformed by training a model for a specific data domain. Otherwise, there is no need to use DSC since every data source can be coded by a well-known generic codec.

2. We mentioned peak-to-noise-ratio (PSNR) in the previous abstract. In the revised version, we have also mentioned it  in the experiment section.

3. We have explicitly labeled the figures in the revised version. We have made the font size of the labels on the figures consistent, as otherwise some labels will overlap the lines on figures.

4. We do not show the compressed images because we find it difficult to visualize the differences unless we enlarge the figures. Since our main focus is not to show that we outperform generic codecs, due to page limit we will conduct experiments to address this part later.

content.title: To all reviewers
content.comment:
Thank you for your time and helpful comments. We have revised our previous submission with the following major changes.
1. We added experiments and figures for measuring the correlation among MNIST splitting by random subsets and class labels.
2. We added experiments and a figure for illustrating data sources split by random subsets.
3. We added a more detailed discussion in the experiment section.
